interactive.title: The glass box
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: Fourteen small screens follow. Some show an idea. The rest ask you to try it. The main picture is a small steel bracket inside a clear glass box. The bracket has a flat base. An upright plate stands along the back edge of the base. A round hole runs front to back through the upright, in its left half. A slot with rounded ends runs down through the base, in its right half. A thin triangular rib in the middle joins the base to the upright. Turn the bracket with your finger to see it from any side. The rule. Each view is what you see looking square through one face of the box. The front view shows width and height. The view from above shows width and depth. The view from the left end shows depth and height. An Unfold button opens the box out flat round the wall the front view lies on. In first angle, each view is cast onto the wall behind the part. So the view from above swings down below the front view. The view from the left end swings out to its right. A First angle and Third angle switch changes the rule. In third angle, each view is drawn on the wall between you and the part. So the view from above swings up above the front view. The view from the left end swings out to its left. Thin pale lines run between the views. They show that the views line up and share their sizes. The projection symbol sits in one corner. It is a cone with its tip cut off, drawn by the rule it names. Its end view, two circles, looks at the cone's narrow end. So in first angle, the circles sit by the cone's wide end. In third angle, they sit by its narrow end. The lines. A solid line is an edge you can see. A dashed line is a hidden edge. A thin chain line marks a centre. Where two lines fall on each other, the visible edge is drawn over the hidden one. Tap any line in a view and the edge it stands for lights on the bracket. In the front view, the hole is a circle and the slot's ends are dashed. A Cut switch shows a cutting plane you drag left and right through the bracket. On the front view, it shows as a chain line, thick at its ends, with arrows and the letters A–A. Section A–A takes the end view's place. Every face the plane cuts is hatched. The one exception is the rib, when the plane runs along its middle. The sizes. A Sizes switch writes the sizes on, in millimetres, with a title block. The base is 80 long. The bracket is 60 high. The hole is Ø12. Its centre is 40 ± 0.2 above the base's underside. The slot is 25 ± 0.1 long. Tap a size and its limits show beside it. The title block gives the drawing number, its issue letter, the units, the projection symbol and the scale, 1 : 5. On your screen the picture is sized to fit. Once the box is unfolded, the bracket shrinks to a small turnable copy above the sheet. At phone width, the switches wrap with no word split. Every label is at least 12 px. Screen by screen. Screen 1, show, One part, several views: the bracket in its box, turned a little. Words: "A part is solid, but a sheet is flat. One picture of a part can hide what lies behind it. So a drawing shows the part from several sides, each seen square-on." Then "Turn it with your finger." Read: the bracket turned to show its upright with the hole, its base with the slot, and the rib between them. Still: the bracket turned to a three-quarter view from the front left, above. Screen 2, do, What a view loses: the bracket and its front view beside it. "You look square at the front of the bracket. Which of its sizes does the front view not show?" Choices: Its depth, front to back (right); Its width, end to end; Its height. Hint on width: "The front view runs from the left end to the right end. That is the width." Hint on height: "The front view runs from the base's underside to the top of the upright." Why: looking square-on, every point along your line of sight lands on the same spot. So the depth folds away. A view keeps two of the three sizes. That is why a drawing usually needs at least two views. After Check, an arrow along the depth lights on the bracket. Screen 3, show, Unfold the box: first angle. Words: "Picture the bracket inside a glass box. In first angle, each view is cast onto the wall behind the part, on the far side from you. Open the box out flat, and the view from above lands below the front view." Then "Tap Unfold." Read: the box lies open and flat. The front view is in the middle. The view from above is below it. The view from the left end is on its right. The first-angle symbol sits in a corner. Still: Unfold on. Screen 4, do, Where does it go?: first angle, unfolded, the front view and the view from above in place, three empty frames beside and over the front view. "The sheet uses first angle. You look at the bracket from its left end. Where does that view go?" Choices: To the right of the front view (right); To the left of the front view; Above the front view. Hint on left: "That would put it on the near side. In first angle, the view is cast onto the wall behind the part." Hint on above: "Views from the ends sit beside the front view, in line with it." Why: from the left end, the view falls on the wall to the right of the part. Open the box flat and that wall lies to the right of the front view. The end view lines up with the front view and shares its height. After Check, the end view swings into place. Then Fold up closes the box round the bracket again. Screen 5, show, The other rule: the first-angle sheet. Words: "Third angle draws each view on the wall between you and the part. So the view from above sits above the front view instead. The projection symbol names the rule. It is a cone, drawn by that rule. In first angle, its circles sit by the cone's wide end. In third angle, they sit by its narrow end." Then "Tap Third angle." Read: the first-angle sheet glides up, and the third-angle sheet sits below it. In third angle, the view from above is above the front view. The view from the left end is on its left. Each sheet has its own symbol. Still: Third angle on, both sheets shown. Screen 6, do, Read the symbol: a third-angle sheet with its symbol, the front view, and one other view on its right. "Read this sheet's projection symbol. A view of the bracket sits to the right of the front view. Which side was it seen from?" Choices: The right end (right); The left end; Above. Hint on the left end: "That is where first angle puts it. Look again at the symbol." Hint on above: "Views from above or below sit over or under the front view, not beside it." Why: the circles sit by the cone's narrow end, so the sheet is third angle. Third angle draws each view on the wall between you and the part. Seen from the right end, that wall is on the right. Opened flat, it stays on the right. After Check, the third-angle symbol rings. Screen 7, show, Lines that mean something: first angle, unfolded, Sizes off. Words: "A thick solid line is an edge you can see. A dashed line is an edge hidden inside or behind the part. A thin chain line marks the centre of a hole or slot. It runs long, short, long." Then "Tap a line to find its edge." Read: in the front view, the two short dashed lines in the base are lit. On the bracket, the slot's ends light up inside the base. Still: the front view's dashed lines tapped. Screen 8, do, Sketch it: first angle, unfolded, the view from above blank. "On paper, sketch the bracket seen from above. How does the hole through the upright show in that view?" Choices: Two dashed lines, with a chain line between (right); A full circle; Two solid lines. Hint on a full circle: "You see the circle only looking along the hole. From above, you look across it." Hint on solid lines: "The hole is inside the upright, under its top face. Is it an edge you can see?" Why: from above, you look down onto the upright's top face. The hole runs front to back underneath it. Its sides are edges hidden behind material, so they are dashed. The chain line marks its centre. After Check, the view from above is drawn in, so you can compare it with your sketch. Screen 9, show, Cut it open: Cut on, the plane through the hole. Words: "To show the inside, picture the part cut along a plane, with the near piece lifted away. A chain line, thick at its ends, marks the cut. Its arrows show which way you look. The section view hatches each cut face with thin sloping lines. A rib cut along its length is left plain." Then "Drag the cutting plane." Read: the plane cuts through the hole. In section A–A, the base and the upright are hatched. The upright has a gap where the hole is. Still: the plane through the hole. Screen 10, do, Hatched or plain: Cut on, the plane along the middle of the rib, the section unhatched. "The plane now runs down the middle of the rib. Which cut faces are hatched in section A–A?" Choices: The base and the upright only (right); The base, the upright and the rib; The rib only. Hint on all three: "The rib is cut too. But a rib cut along its length is left plain." Hint on the rib only: "The base and the upright are cut too. Every cut face here is hatched, except a rib cut along its length." Why: hatched, the rib would make the corner look solid, as if the metal were thick there. Left plain, with its outline drawn, it reads as a thin rib. After Check, the hatching fills in. Screen 11, show, Sizes, limits and scale: Sizes on. Words: "Work to the sizes written on the drawing, here in millimetres. A size of 25 ± 0.1 means any length from 24.9 to 25.1 mm is right. The scale 1 : 5 says the picture is drawn a fifth of the part's size." Then "Tap the slot's size." Read: the slot's length is lit. Its limits, 24.9 and 25.1 mm, sit beside it. The title block shows the scale, the units, the projection symbol, the drawing number and its issue letter. Still: the slot's size tapped. Screen 12, do, mixed, typed, The smallest that passes: Sizes on, the hole's centre lit. "The hole's centre is 40 ± 0.2 above the base's underside. What is the smallest height that still passes?" A typed answer: 39.8, in mm, to one decimal place. Slips: 40.2, "That is the largest height that passes. Take 0.2 off instead."; 39.6, "That takes off 0.4. The limit is 0.2 either side of 40."; 40, "That is the size aimed at. Any height down to the lower limit still passes." Hint: "± 0.2 means 0.2 either side of 40." Why: the smallest that passes is 40 − 0.2, which is 39.8 mm. The largest is 40 + 0.2, which is 40.2 mm. After Check, both limits show beside the size. Screen 13, do, mixed, typed, Drawn to scale: Sizes on, the base's size lit. "The base is 80 long. The scale is 1 : 5. How long is the base drawn on the sheet?" A typed answer: 16, in mm, a whole number. Slips: 400, "That multiplies it. At 1 : 5, the picture is a fifth of the part's size."; 80, "That is the part's size. The picture is drawn at a fifth of that." Hint: "At 1 : 5, each 1 mm on the sheet stands for 5 mm of the part." Why: 80 ÷ 5 is 16 mm. Still work to the written 80. It is the part's true size. After Check, a ruler lies along the drawn base. Screen 14, do, mixed, Which part?: a first-angle sheet of a second bracket, front view and the view from above below it, Sizes off, and three small solids labelled Part A, Part B and Part C. Part A is the bracket so far, with its slot. Part B has a round hole down through the base in place of the slot. Part C has a round peg standing on the base in place of the slot. The sheet shows Part B. In the view from above, the base has a solid circle with chain lines crossing at its centre. In the front view, two dashed lines run down through the base's thickness, with a chain line between. "Which part do these views show?" Choices: Part B (right); Part A; Part C. Hint on Part A: "Look at the view from above. Is the outline in the base long or round?" Hint on Part C: "In the front view, the lines in the base are dashed. They are hidden inside it, not standing up from it." Why: from above, the feature is a circle, so it is round. In the front view, its sides are dashed and stay within the base. So it is a hole through the base. It takes both views to tell. After Check, Part B turns to match the views.
interactive.ignores: The bracket turns, opens and cuts as a picture. On your screen it is sized to fit, not drawn to 1 : 5. Only a few sizes are written. A real drawing gives every size needed to make the part, each once. The bracket has no threads, chamfers, surface finish or material note. Real drawings carry these. The only section here is a full cut on one plane, square to the bracket's length. Real drawings also use views at an angle, part sections and drawings of whole assemblies. Nothing here shows how to make a drawing or use a CAD system.

explain.text:
An engineering drawing shows one part's shape, seen square-on from several sides. A fixed rule sets out the views, so you can rebuild the part in your head. A schematic maps what is joined to what. An engineering drawing is different. It shows the shape and size of one part. A general arrangement drawing, or GA, shows how the parts of a whole machine fit together. You will meet them for machinery.

A part is solid, but a sheet is flat. So why not one picture? Look square at the front of a part. Every point along your line of sight lands on the same spot. So the front view shows width and height, but not depth. Each view keeps two of the three sizes and loses the third. That is why a drawing usually needs at least two views, and often three.

Picture the part inside a glass box. In [[first angle]], each view is cast onto the wall behind the part, on the far side from where you look. Open the box out flat round the front view. The view from above lands below it. The view from the left end lands on its right. Third angle draws each view on the wall between you and the part instead. So the view from above sits above the front view. The view from the left end sits on its left. Both rules are in use, so you need to read both.[^1] A [[projection symbol]] on the sheet says which rule it follows. It is a cone with its tip cut off, drawn by the rule it names. Its end view, two circles, looks at the cone's narrow end. In first angle, that view goes to the far side, by the wide end. In third angle, it sits by the narrow end. Read a first-angle sheet as third angle, and you take the view from the left end as the view from the right. The part then comes out mirrored. Under either rule, the views line up and share their sizes. The view from above is as wide as the front view. It sits square below or above it.

The lines carry meaning too. A thick solid line is an edge you can see. A dashed line is an edge hidden inside or behind the part. A thin chain line marks the centre of a hole or a slot. Its pattern is long dash, short dash, long dash. Where two fall on each other, the visible edge is drawn over the hidden one. A hidden edge is drawn over a centre line. So take one feature at a time, and follow it from view to view. Say a hole is a circle in the front view and dashed lines from above. Then it runs front to back, inside the part.

To show the inside, a [[section view]] pictures the part cut along a plane, with the near piece lifted away. A line on another view marks the plane. Its arrows show which way you look. Cut faces are hatched with thin sloping lines. But a thin rib cut along its length is left plain. So are shafts and bolts. Hatched, the rib would make the corner look solid, as if the metal were thick there.

Sizes are written on the drawing. They are the part's true sizes, so work to them. A tolerance says how far a size may stray. A size of 25 ± 0.1 means any length from 24.9 to 25.1 mm is right. The scale says how big the picture is against the part. At 1 : 5, it is a fifth of full size. The title block usually holds the scale, the units, the projection symbol, the drawing number and its issue. Check the issue is the current one before you work from it.

**Read the projection symbol first. Then follow each feature across the views. Each view shows two sizes, and together they fix the shape.**

analogy.text: You know this from a building's drawings. The floor plan shows where each socket sits along the walls. But it cannot show how high it is, unless a written note gives it. The wall elevation, seen square-on to that wall, shows the height. You put the two together to fix each socket in the room. A part's views work the same way. Each one loses a size, and another gives it back.
analogy.breaks: Building plans are often on separate sheets, each labelled by name. You read them from inside the room. A part's views usually share one sheet, and you see them from outside. Their places follow first or third angle. Put a view in the wrong place and you read the part the wrong way round.

practice.text:
- Check the title block first. Read the drawing number and its issue, and make sure it is the current one.
- Read the projection symbol. It tells you where each view sits round the front view.
- Find the front view. Name each other view by the side it was seen from.
- Take one feature at a time. Follow it from view to view along the lines they share.
- Read the lines. Thick solid is an edge you can see. Dashed is a hidden edge. A thin chain line is usually a centre.
- On a section, find the cutting plane line and its arrows. Hatching is cut material. A plain rib inside a section has been cut along its length.
- Work to the written sizes and their tolerances. They are the part's true sizes.

**Rule of thumb:** a single square-on view hides one size. So judge each feature from at least two views.

**Worked example:** the bracket. The symbol says first angle, so the view from above is below the front view. The hole is Ø12. It is a circle in the front view and dashed lines from above. So it runs front to back through the upright. Its centre is 40 ± 0.2 above the underside. Any height from 39.8 to 40.2 mm passes. The base is 80 long. At 1 : 5, it is drawn 16 mm long, but you still work to 80.

**Common mistakes**
- Placing the views by the wrong rule, without reading the symbol.
- Reading a dashed hidden edge as an edge you can see.
- Reading a centre line as an edge.
- Judging a feature from one view alone.
- Taking a plain rib in a section as uncut.
- Taking a size from the picture instead of the written size.
- Taking the size aimed at as the only size that passes.
- Working from an old issue of the drawing.

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is each view riding on its wall to a fixed place round the front view, and changing sides with the rule, when you unfold the glass box.

checks.label: Components are 3-dimensional, but documents and screens are 2-dimensional: the bracket has three sizes, and every view of it is flat, a set of lines in two directions only
Each view keeps two of the three sizes: the front view spans 80 by 60 (width, height), the view from above 80 by 40 (width, depth), the end view 40 by 60 (depth, height)
Either first or third angle can be chosen, and both should be understood: the page draws the bracket by each rule, each with all three views
Unfolded, first angle puts the view from above below the front view and the left-end view on its right; third angle puts them above and on its left; each view is the same picture in both, only moved
The views line up and share their sizes: from above is exactly as wide as the front view and square under or over it; the end view is exactly as tall and square beside it, in both rules

Hidden edges are dashed and visible ones solid: in the front view the hole is a solid circle and the slot two dashed lines; from above the slot is a solid outline and the hole two dashed lines with a chain line between

The cutting plane sets the section: through the hole (20 along) the upright shows a 12 gap and the base none; through the slot (60 along) the base shows a 10 gap; along the rib (40 along) the rib is cut but nothing hatched lies inside it
The projection symbol is a cone drawn by its own rule: its end view looks at the narrow end, so first angle puts the two circles by the wide end and third angle by the narrow end
Worked by hand: 25 ± 0.1 allows 24.9 to 25.1; 40 ± 0.2 allows 39.8 to 40.2; at 1 : 5 the 80 base is drawn 16; the fields ask exactly these, with their slips

Only Part B matches the sheet: from above its feature is round, where Part A has a slot 25 long and 10 wide; in the front view its lines are dashed and stay within the base, where Part C has solid lines standing above it
Seen from the front left, above, the bracket shows its front, its top and its left end, and hides its back, its right end and its underside

Before an answer nothing gives it away: screen 4 shows no end view, screen 6 no view labels and no ring, screen 8 an empty frame for the view from above, screen 10 no hatching, screen 12 no limits, screen 14 no ring and Part B unturned, and no puzzle shows its switches
Every demonstration settles within 4.5 s, every answer's motion within 3 s, and the box unfolds in 3.6 s

applied.problem: Three rules are stated too absolutely: some parts are drawn in one view with a note; thin solid lines are also dimension and hatching lines; and shafts and bolts cut along their length are left plain too, not just ribs.

"Solid is an edge you can see" and "a chain line is a centre" are too absolute: thin solid lines also mark sizes and hatching, and a chain line thick at its ends is a cutting plane, as the next step says.

It says the box always unfolds round its back wall, where the front view lies, but in third angle the front view is on the front wall; it also says solid lines are edges and a drawing needs two views, both too absolute.
A floor plan often gives socket heights in a written note, so "it cannot show how high it is" is too absolute for an electrician who reads them.
A part drawing can run to several sheets, so "a part's views share one sheet" is too absolute.
